Tool calling: delta aggregation, partial arguments, parallel tool calls
Structured output / JSON schema validation and retry strategies
POC success criteria and next steps
summary: Northpeak evaluated Redwood’s streaming + tool calling behavior for a workflow that mixes real-time UI updates with function/tool execution and strict JSON outputs. The team asked detailed questions about event naming/ordering (token_delta vs tool_call_delta), how to handle partial tool arguments during streaming, whether parallel tools are supported, and what retry/validation patterns Redwood recommends for structured outputs. Redwood clarified that examples are being refreshed to align on a canonical event model and offered to share the canonical examples and troubleshooting guidance (disconnects, partial args, schema mismatch).

transcript:
Meeting: Streaming + tool calling deep dive (Redwood Inference x Northpeak)
Date: 2026-01-22
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai
Duration: ~52 minutes

Attendees
- Nikhil Sharma (Redwood Inference)
- Ibrahim Khan (Redwood Inference)
- Henry Cho (Redwood Inference)
- Sarah Ling (Northpeak)
- Tom Reyes (Northpeak)
- Priya Natarajan (Northpeak)


[00:00] Nikhil Sharma: Cool, I think we’re good to start. Sarah, Tom, Priya—thanks for making time. The goal today was just to go deeper on streaming semantics and tools, because I know you’re evaluating a couple options.

[00:14] Priya Natarajan: Yep. We’ve got a product review next week. We want to be confident the event model won’t surprise us.

[00:22] Sarah Ling: Yeah and we have a UI that’s streaming tokens to users, but also we do tool execution. The “function calling” stuff is where it gets weird, honestly.

[00:32] Nikhil Sharma: Totally. Ibrahim is our tech lead for SDK parity and examples, and Henry’s the PM owning tools and structured outputs.

[00:40] Ibrahim Khan: Hi everyone.

[00:41] Henry Cho: Hey.

[00:45] Tom Reyes: Hey.

[00:47] Nikhil Sharma: Sarah, you want to start with your current stack and where you’ve gotten stuck?

[00:55] Sarah Ling: Sure. We run a gateway in our VPC, and today we stream over SSE. Sometimes corporate proxies buffer, so we’re already sensitive to “does it actually flush.” But the bigger pain is tool calling. We see partial JSON arguments and then the sample code we copied from a vendor just does JSON.parse on every chunk and it explodes.

[01:15] Tom Reyes: And then you don’t know if you should retry the tool, retry the model call, or just wait.

[01:20] Ibrahim Khan: Yep, that’s like the number one footgun.

[01:24] Henry Cho: We’ve been tightening that up in docs and examples—basically the message is: don’t parse tool args until the tool call is finalized.

[01:33] Sarah Ling: So what is “finalized” in Redwood terms? Like, what’s the actual event sequence.

[01:39] Ibrahim Khan: Let me describe it at a conceptual level, and then we can talk payload shapes. In streaming you get a series of events. There are token deltas—think incremental text. There are tool call deltas—incremental updates to a tool call object, including arguments. And then there’s a terminal event which indicates the response is complete, like “final response object,” plus usage.

[02:02] Tom Reyes: When you say “terminal event,” is it like OpenAI’s “done” message? Like a literal [DONE] sentinel.

[02:09] Ibrahim Khan: Similar concept, but we recommend people treat it as “response.completed” or “message.completed” event. I don’t want to overfit to names because some SDKs wrap it, but the idea is: you should have a clear point where tool calls are complete and safe to dispatch.

[02:26] Sarah Ling: Wait, you said “some SDKs wrap it.” That’s kinda my worry. We’re using TypeScript and Go. We don’t want three different loops.

[02:36] Ibrahim Khan: Totally fair. One of the things we’re doing right now is a canonical examples refresh so the flow is the same across Python, TS, and Go. The event taxonomy is consistent even if the code looks a bit different.

[02:52] Nikhil Sharma: That’s actually why we offered this call. We’ve seen drift in older snippets and we’re cleaning it up.

[03:00] Priya Natarajan: Can we get concrete: if the model decides to call a tool, do we still get token streaming? Or is it paused.

[03:09] Henry Cho: Good question. It depends on what the model is producing. Typically you’ll see either (a) assistant text deltas, or (b) tool call deltas. Some models will “think” in a way that looks like text, but we don’t expose hidden chain-of-thought. You might see a short assistant message like “Let me check that” and then tool call deltas.

[03:29] Sarah Ling: Ok. And if it’s a tool call, how does it show up? Is it one object with id + name + arguments.

[03:36] Ibrahim Khan: Yes. There’s an id for the tool call, the tool name, and arguments which are a string that accumulates. The important part: arguments may be emitted in chunks that are not valid JSON until the end.

[03:52] Tom Reyes: So you’re saying it’s literally a string stream, not a JSON stream.

[03:56] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. Think “append-only string fragments.” You aggregate and only parse when the tool call is complete.

[04:05] Sarah Ling: How do we know it’s complete? Is there an explicit flag.

[04:10] Henry Cho: In the stream you’ll get an event indicating the tool call is finished, or you’ll get a final message object where the tool call is present with complete arguments. In practice we recommend: accumulate tool args by tool_call_id, and only dispatch when you receive the “tool_call.completed” or when the assistant message is marked complete.

[04:30] Tom Reyes: So you’re aligning to “tool_call_id.” That’s good.

[04:35] Priya Natarajan: And parallel tools? Like multiple tool calls in one assistant turn.

[04:40] Henry Cho: Supported. The model can emit multiple tool calls. You’ll see deltas interleaved, so that id is key.

[04:49] Sarah Ling: Interleaved as in: call A gets some args, then call B, then back to A?

[04:54] Henry Cho: Yep.

[04:56] Sarah Ling: That’s exactly where our current code breaks.

[05:00] Ibrahim Khan: Right, because people often assume it’s one tool call start to finish.

[05:05] Tom Reyes: Do you support “tool choice” like forcing a specific tool.

[05:11] Henry Cho: Yes. You can set a policy: auto, required, or force a specific tool. Again, terminology differs across providers, but conceptually yes.

[05:21] Nikhil Sharma: To zoom out—your use case is: stream to UI, if tool call occurs, execute it server-side, then continue streaming the final answer, correct?

[05:31] Sarah Ling: Correct. And we also care about structured output. Like we want the final assistant response to be JSON matching a schema. But we still want streaming for the user experience.

[05:42] Ibrahim Khan: That’s the hardest combo because you can’t validate partial JSON reliably.

[05:48] Tom Reyes: Exactly. And we’ve seen “JSON mode” from others where it still produces garbage sometimes.

[05:55] Henry Cho: So Redwood’s guidance is: if you truly need schema-valid JSON, treat the stream as UI only, and only validate at the end. If validation fails, do a targeted retry with the model using the same schema and include the validation error.

[06:13] Sarah Ling: Is that in your docs? Because I want that pattern, not hand-wavy “retry.”

[06:18] Henry Cho: Yes—well, we’re updating it. The new docs include a concrete “validate + retry-on-parse-failure” pattern. We also suggest setting a max retries and logging the invalid output with redaction.

[06:34] Priya Natarajan: What’s the failure mode when schema mismatch happens? Is there an explicit API error.

[06:41] Henry Cho: If you request structured output with a schema, the gateway can reject obviously invalid schema definitions up front. But the model output itself might not conform; that’s not always catchable server-side until the full output is generated. So you’ll get a completed response, then your client validation fails.

[06:58] Tom Reyes: So you’re not doing server-side enforcement.

[07:02] Henry Cho: Not in a way that guarantees correctness for every model. We provide recommended client validation. Some customers do a second pass “repair” call.

[07:13] Sarah Ling: Ok, so the canonical pattern is: stream tokens, buffer final, validate, maybe retry.

[07:19] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly.

[07:22] Tom Reyes: Do you have example code that does the delta aggregation properly for tools, and then uses the tool result to continue.

[07:29] Ibrahim Khan: Yes. That’s part of the canonical examples set—single tool and parallel tools. And it’s the same flow across languages.

[07:40] Sarah Ling: Can we talk about event naming? Because we’ve been burned by “delta” meaning different things.

[07:46] Ibrahim Khan: Sure. In our canonical model we try to keep it simple: 
- “token_delta” (or content delta) events: incremental assistant text.
- “tool_call_delta” events: partial updates to a tool call object.
- “response_completed” event: signals you have the final response.
And the SDK abstracts that into a stream iterator. But you always have a way to (a) handle deltas, (b) detect final, and (c) access the final assembled response.

[08:18] Tom Reyes: Do you send “usage” only at the end?

[08:21] Ibrahim Khan: Yes, usage is finalized at the end.

[08:24] Sarah Ling: What about errors mid-stream? Like disconnects.

[08:29] Nikhil Sharma: Great topic. We’ve seen disconnects from proxies, load balancers, or client timeouts. Our docs now call out: set read timeouts appropriately, disable proxy buffering if possible, and treat disconnect as retriable depending on idempotency.

[08:47] Tom Reyes: Is there a way to resume a stream from an offset.

[08:51] Ibrahim Khan: Not a true resume from token N today. Some customers do application-level checkpointing. For example: if a stream drops, you reissue the request with the same conversation state, and you might include the partial text you already showed as context to avoid duplication. But there’s no official “resume cursor” in the API.

[09:13] Sarah Ling: That’s kinda important. We can handle it though.

[09:18] Priya Natarajan: I’m less worried about resume. I’m worried about the tool dispatch. Like if a disconnect happens while tool args are mid-flight, we could accidentally execute a tool with incomplete args.

[09:30] Henry Cho: Exactly. That’s why our guidance is: never execute a tool until the tool call is marked complete. And even then, validate arguments against a schema you control.

[09:43] Sarah Ling: So you recommend schema validation for tool args too.

[09:47] Henry Cho: Yes. Even if the model “should” call it correctly, you should validate. Also use an allowlist of tools—don’t just execute arbitrary tool names.

[10:00] Tom Reyes: Good. We had security raise that.

[10:03] Priya Natarajan: We also have a rule: no shell, no raw network. Only internal service calls.

[10:09] Henry Cho: That’s aligned with what we recommend.

[10:12] Ibrahim Khan: In the sample code we avoid unsafe tools. It’s usually like “get_weather” as a stand-in, but the pattern is what matters.

[10:22] Sarah Ling: Ok. Switching gears: parallel tools. Do you have any throttle guidance? Like don’t execute 20 tools at once.

[10:31] Henry Cho: Yeah, we show concurrency control in the TypeScript example—like a small pool. In Go you can use errgroup with a limit, or a semaphore.

[10:41] Tom Reyes: Nice.

[10:43] Sarah Ling: Another thing: we saw another provider stream tool args as JSON patches. Do you do that?

[10:50] Ibrahim Khan: No, we keep it simpler: string deltas. JSON patches look nice but they’re harder to implement across SDKs.

[10:58] Sarah Ling: Got it.

[11:00] Nikhil Sharma: Maybe it’d help if you describe one of your real tool calls. Like what’s the tool signature.

[11:07] Sarah Ling: It’s basically a “search_knowledge_base” tool. Args: query, filters, maybe customer_id, time_range. And the output is a JSON array of hits.

[11:18] Tom Reyes: We also have a “create_ticket” tool but we gate it behind user confirmation.

[11:24] Henry Cho: Great. That’s a good best practice—human-in-the-loop for actions.

[11:28] Sarah Ling: So in our server, we want to stream tokens until the model decides it needs to call search. Then we execute search. Then we send results back to the model and stream the answer.

[11:41] Ibrahim Khan: That’s the canonical loop: model -> tool calls -> tool execution -> model continuation.

[11:48] Tom Reyes: In your API is that “two requests” or “one request” that pauses.

[11:53] Ibrahim Khan: Two requests in most setups. The first streaming response yields tool calls. You execute tools. Then you send a follow-up request including tool results as messages.

[12:06] Sarah Ling: Ok. And structured output, where does that fit? Only on the last request.

[12:12] Henry Cho: Usually yes. You might require structured output on the final assistant message, not on the tool-calling turn.

[12:20] Priya Natarajan: Can you also do structured output for tool args.

[12:24] Henry Cho: You can define tool parameter schemas, yes, but you should still validate because the stream is partial.

[12:33] Tom Reyes: So if the tool schema is JSON schema-ish, you’re basically telling model what to produce.

[12:39] Henry Cho: Exactly.

[12:41] Sarah Ling: Ok I’m going to ask a nitpicky thing: if tool args come as partial chunks, what if we receive something like "{\"query\": \"foo" and then we time out. We should not execute. But do we store it.

[12:56] Ibrahim Khan: You can store it for debugging, but treat it as untrusted. Also make sure logs are redacted because arguments may include user data.

[13:06] Nikhil Sharma: We can share a troubleshooting doc on that too. It calls out proxy buffering and timeouts.

[13:14] Tom Reyes: Do you have recommended timeout defaults? Our Go HTTP client defaults are… not great.

[13:21] Ibrahim Khan: For Go: set a request context deadline that’s longer than your expected generation. And don’t use a low idle timeout on proxies. Also, you want to configure the response body reader to handle long-lived connections.

[13:36] Tom Reyes: Ok.

[13:38] Sarah Ling: Switching to retries. If validation fails on structured output, what’s your recommended prompt pattern? Like do we send “here’s the schema error, fix it.”

[13:51] Henry Cho: Yep. The best performing pattern we’ve seen is: provide the schema again, provide the previous invalid JSON, provide the validation errors (like “field X missing, expected integer”), and instruct it to output only valid JSON.

[14:07] Sarah Ling: And does the model sometimes hallucinate extra fields anyway.

[14:12] Henry Cho: Yes. That’s why you cap retries and maybe fall back to a more reliable model variant.

[14:18] Nikhil Sharma: That’s another point: Redwood lets you define fallback policies. If the first model fails schema validation twice, you can try a stricter model.

[14:28] Priya Natarajan: Is that built-in or do we implement.

[14:31] Nikhil Sharma: Mostly app-level today, but we can advise. The docs talk about it as a recommended pattern.

[14:40] Sarah Ling: Ok. On the tool side, do you have any server-side validation of tool args before you forward events.

[14:47] Henry Cho: We don’t mutate the stream. We treat it as model output. We can validate schema definitions, but not partial args. So we push validation to the tool dispatcher.

[14:59] Tom Reyes: Makes sense.

[15:01] Sarah Ling: Ok can we get a sample event payload. Like just an example.

[15:07] Ibrahim Khan: I can describe it. You’ll see something like: event type tool_call_delta, id "call_123", name "search_knowledge_base", arguments_delta "{\"query\":\"refund policy"…". Then subsequent deltas append. Eventually you get tool_call_completed with full arguments string.

[15:27] Sarah Ling: Do you ever send “arguments” as full replacement, not delta.

[15:31] Ibrahim Khan: No, we standardize on delta semantics. But you shouldn’t assume the delta is one token; it can be any chunk.

[15:41] Tom Reyes: And for token deltas it’s also chunks.

[15:45] Ibrahim Khan: Correct.

[15:48] Priya Natarajan: If you have both tool calls and text, do you interleave.

[15:54] Henry Cho: Potentially, yes. But most models don’t alternate heavily. Still, clients should handle it.

[16:02] Sarah Ling: So UI streaming might show “thinking” text and then a tool call, and then stop.

[16:09] Henry Cho: Some will.

[16:10] Sarah Ling: We might hide that and just show a spinner.

[16:14] Nikhil Sharma: Many customers do.

[16:17] Tom Reyes: On the structured output piece, do you support JSON schema draft 7 or 2020.

[16:24] Henry Cho: We recommend a conservative subset—objects, arrays, enums, required fields. Avoid super fancy constructs because model compliance drops.

[16:35] Sarah Ling: Like oneOf.

[16:36] Henry Cho: Exactly. oneOf is a nightmare.

[16:40] Tom Reyes: That’s consistent with our experience.

[16:43] Sarah Ling: One more question: some providers have a separate “json mode” which is just “output JSON,” and a separate “structured output” with schema. How do you name it.

[16:56] Henry Cho: We’re aligning on “structured output” for schema-based. We try not to call it JSON mode because that’s ambiguous.

[17:06] Priya Natarajan: Good. Less confusion.

[17:09] Nikhil Sharma: Since you mentioned other vendors—are you evaluating OpenAI direct, or like an aggregator.

[17:17] Priya Natarajan: We’re using a mix. We tried OpenAI and Anthropic. We also looked at Together because we might self-host later. And internally we’ve got a vLLM cluster.

[17:30] Nikhil Sharma: Got it. So portability matters.

[17:33] Sarah Ling: Yeah. We don’t want to rewrite our tool loops per provider.

[17:38] Ibrahim Khan: That’s exactly what we’re trying to solve with consistent docs + SDK flows.

[17:45] Tom Reyes: What about Go vs TS differences. Like do both support the same streaming iterator.

[17:52] Ibrahim Khan: The shapes are consistent. TS uses an async iterator. Go uses a reader loop with context cancellation. But the logic is identical: switch on event type, accumulate by id, finalize at the end.

[18:09] Tom Reyes: And errors—like parse error if we try too early—your example avoids it.

[18:14] Ibrahim Khan: Yes.

[18:16] Sarah Ling: Can you also confirm: we should never trust the model to choose the tool name. Like it should be allowlisted.

[18:23] Henry Cho: Right. Allowlist the tool names you expose. If the model tries to call something else, treat it as an error.

[18:31] Priya Natarajan: Ok. That’ll help me with security review.

[18:35] Nikhil Sharma: Speaking of security, if you move forward, we can also share details on VPC deployments, but today we’ll keep it to streaming semantics.

[18:44] Sarah Ling: Yeah. One thing: if the stream disconnects mid-response, do you have metrics or error codes that tell why.

[18:54] Nikhil Sharma: We’re adding better observability around disconnect reasons. On the client, you usually see network-level errors, but we’re improving server metrics. We can share best practices though: keep-alives, proxy buffering off.

[19:12] Tom Reyes: Ok.

[19:14] Sarah Ling: Let’s talk about POC. We want to test: 1) streaming UI is smooth, 2) tool args deltas don’t break us, 3) structured output validity rate is high.

[19:27] Nikhil Sharma: That’s great. What’s your SLA target.

[19:31] Priya Natarajan: For streaming we want first token under 500ms ideally. But it’s ok if it’s 800. More important is we don’t hang.

[19:43] Tom Reyes: And tool call should happen within like 2 seconds because otherwise the user thinks it’s stuck.

[19:49] Nikhil Sharma: Makes sense.

[19:51] Ibrahim Khan: For tools, sometimes the model takes time to decide. But we can tune prompts.

[19:57] Sarah Ling: Another question: do you support a “tool call only” response where the model emits no content.

[20:04] Henry Cho: Yes. It can be a tool-only assistant turn.

[20:09] Sarah Ling: Ok.

[20:10] Tom Reyes: For the structured output: if the schema mismatch happens, does Redwood return a special error we can key on.

[20:18] Henry Cho: Not as a server error, since it’s a client validation failure. But we recommend you raise your own “SCHEMA_VALIDATION_FAILED” error and attach the model output and the validation details.

[20:33] Sarah Ling: Got it.

[20:35] Nikhil Sharma: Maybe we should align on what you’ll want from us after today.

[20:40] Sarah Ling: I need canonical example code. Specifically TS and Go. I want the loop that does: stream events, collect tool args, execute allowlisted tools, then do a second call and validate JSON output with a retry.

[20:58] Ibrahim Khan: Yep.

[20:59] Henry Cho: We can send that.

[21:02] Tom Reyes: Also, I’d like sample payloads. Like a literal snippet of event lines.

[21:09] Ibrahim Khan: I can send sample payloads.

[21:12] Priya Natarajan: And anything about disconnects and proxy buffering. Our customers are in finance, they sit behind proxies.

[21:20] Nikhil Sharma: Understood.

[21:22] (crosstalk)

[21:23] Sarah Ling: Sorry, one more thing. Parallel tool calls—if we execute them in parallel, can we send tool results back in any order.

[21:32] Henry Cho: Yes, as long as you associate them to the correct tool_call_id when you send back tool results.

[21:40] Tom Reyes: Good.

[21:41] Sarah Ling: Ok.

[21:44] Nikhil Sharma: Great. We’ve got about 30 minutes left. We can either go deeper into structured output schemas, or do more around timeouts and retries.

[21:53] Sarah Ling: Let’s do structured outputs a bit more.

[21:56] Henry Cho: Ok. The key gotchas: keep schemas small, avoid optional fields where possible, use enums sparingly, and keep descriptions short. Models sometimes treat long descriptions as extra output instructions.

[22:14] Tom Reyes: Interesting.

[22:15] Sarah Ling: And in the retry, do you change temperature.

[22:21] Henry Cho: Usually set temperature lower for retries. Also you can include “output must be strictly valid JSON, no markdown.”

[22:32] Sarah Ling: And do you ever do a “repair model” like a smaller model.

[22:36] Henry Cho: Some do. But often using a more reliable model variant for repair works.

[22:44] Priya Natarajan: Cost wise that’s ok, if it’s rare.

[22:47] Nikhil Sharma: Exactly.

[22:49] Tom Reyes: What’s your recommendation for logging invalid JSON. We can’t log PII.

[22:56] Ibrahim Khan: Log a hashed request id, store the invalid output in a secure store with retention controls, or redact fields. But don’t dump raw customer data in app logs.

[23:09] Sarah Ling: Ok.

[23:11] Henry Cho: Another thing: be explicit about schema versioning. If you change schemas and old code is still in the wild, you can get mismatch errors.

[23:23] Sarah Ling: That’s real. We had a copy/paste snippet from old docs at another vendor and it used a schema that didn’t match what the model actually returned.

[23:33] Nikhil Sharma: That’s why we’re refreshing ours.

[23:36] Tom Reyes: On tool args: do you recommend also having a schema for tool args separate from tool definition.

[23:44] Henry Cho: Typically the tool definition includes parameter schema. But you can also validate against your internal struct.

[23:52] Tom Reyes: In Go we’ll just decode to struct.

[23:55] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly, but again, only after completion.

[24:00] Sarah Ling: Ok. Let’s talk about stream handling. In TypeScript, we have an AbortController for timeouts. If we abort mid-stream, the server sees it as disconnect. Any gotchas.

[24:15] Ibrahim Khan: That’s fine. Just be careful: aborting is not a retry. If you abort after you’ve already executed tools, you need idempotency logic on your side.

[24:27] Sarah Ling: Right. Because you might re-run a tool.

[24:30] Henry Cho: Exactly.

[24:32] Priya Natarajan: We can include a tool execution id.

[24:35] Tom Reyes: Or our internal service is idempotent.

[24:38] Nikhil Sharma: Great.

[24:40] Sarah Ling: Can Redwood provide idempotency keys on the request.

[24:45] Nikhil Sharma: For hosted API we have request ids and you can pass your own idempotency key headers in some contexts. We can follow up with specifics. But app-level idempotency is still recommended.

[25:02] Sarah Ling: Ok.

[25:04] Tom Reyes: Another thing: streaming events. Are they always ordered.

[25:08] Ibrahim Khan: Yes, ordered as produced. But tool deltas can be interleaved by id.

[25:14] Tom Reyes: Understood.

[25:16] Sarah Ling: Ok can we do a quick “walk through” scenario.

[25:20] Henry Cho: Sure.

[25:22] Sarah Ling: User asks: “What’s our refund policy for EU.” Model starts: “Let me look that up” token deltas. Then emits tool call “search_knowledge_base” with args delta chunked. We accumulate. At tool_call_completed, we parse args JSON and validate. Execute tool. Then create new messages with tool result. Second request: structured output required with schema like {answer: string, citations: array}. Stream token deltas but we buffer final output and validate at end. If invalid, retry second request with error. Correct.

[25:59] Henry Cho: That’s perfect.

[26:02] Ibrahim Khan: Yep.

[26:03] Nikhil Sharma: And we can provide snippets for that.

[26:07] Tom Reyes: Nice.

[26:10] Priya Natarajan: How do you handle “silent parse failures.” Like JSON.parse returns something but it’s not what you expect.

[26:18] Henry Cho: That’s why you do schema validation, not just parsing.

[26:23] Sarah Ling: We use Zod in TS.

[26:25] Henry Cho: Great. That’s exactly what our TS example uses.

[26:29] Tom Reyes: In Go we’ll use jsonschema or just manual validation.

[26:34] Ibrahim Khan: We show both patterns.

[26:38] Sarah Ling: Ok.

[26:40] Nikhil Sharma: Any other questions we haven’t hit.

[26:44] Sarah Ling: A bit about performance. Does tool calling affect latency.

[26:48] Nikhil Sharma: There’s the model latency plus the tool latency. We optimize the model serving side (batching, KV cache), but the tool call itself is your infra.

[26:58] Tom Reyes: Right.

[27:00] Sarah Ling: Ok.

[27:02] Priya Natarajan: I’m good.

[27:04] Tom Reyes: I’m good.

[27:06] Nikhil Sharma: Great. Let’s use the remaining time for “what do you need to evaluate” so we can set up next week.

[27:14] Priya Natarajan: We need a crisp doc that we can hand to engineering: how streaming events work, how tool deltas work, how to validate and retry.

[27:26] Nikhil Sharma: Great.

[27:28] Sarah Ling: And some runnable examples. Like copy paste.

[27:31] Ibrahim Khan: That’s the goal.

[27:33] Sarah Ling: Also clarify terminology. Some docs say function calling, some say tool calling.

[27:39] Henry Cho: We’re standardizing on “tool calling.”

[27:42] Tom Reyes: Great.

[27:44] Nikhil Sharma: Ok. We’ll send those. We’re also launching a canonical examples repo and snippet tests so docs don’t drift.

[27:54] Sarah Ling: Good. Drift has been our pain.

[27:58] Nikhil Sharma: Cool. Let’s do recap and next steps.

[28:03] Nikhil Sharma: Ibrahim will share sample event payloads plus the canonical event model write-up. Henry will share structured output JSON schema guidance plus validation + retry pattern. I’ll work with you on staging access for a small test run, and we’ll schedule a follow-up early next week.

[28:23] Sarah Ling: Sounds good.

[28:25] Tom Reyes: Works.

[28:26] Priya Natarajan: Yep.

[28:28] Nikhil Sharma: Great, thanks everyone.
